column2: This cement company’s Tir sales fell; the announcements say it was because of summer power limits, so it’s temporary.
For the year’s profit, count the normal months (about 128 thousand tonnes a month) and put 25% less for the two limited months: about 1,472 thousand tonnes a year.
At the current price, the year’s sales are about 3,390 billion rials. With the company’s usual margin, admin costs and tax, earnings per share come to about 1,525 rials.
The Tir drop is no reason to sell the share, because it’s seasonal and temporary; but it goes into the yearly calculation.
If your shop sells less for a month because the street is being repaired, you don’t sell the shop; you just count the year’s income a little lower.
This holding’s earnings per share went from 400 to 1,100, and channels say “the P/E is only 4”.
But 750 rials of it is a one-off gain from selling shares of one of its subsidiaries.
Lasting profit = 1,100 − 750 = 350 rials. At a price of 4,400, the real P/E is about 12.6, not 4.
For a holding the main measure is the value of its assets (NAV). If it sold the shares below the market price, value was lost.
If this year your salary was 100 and you also sold your car for 200, next year’s income isn’t 300; it’s 100.
Holding B: separate the one-off profit
Announcement: the price of gas (raw material) goes up 15% from next month.
This petrochemical company buys 10,000 billion of gas a year; so 1,500 billion a year in extra cost, that is 25% less operating profit.
9 months of this year are left, so about 1,125 this year and the full amount from next year.
This change repeats every year; so update lasting profit and the payback calculation the same day.
If your shop’s rent goes up 15% from next month, you need to change next year’s profit calculation now, not at the end of the year.
Petrochemical C: news that changes profit
This parts maker has shown growing profit three years in a row.

But the cash from its work is negative, the related carmaker pays later and later (from 6 months of sales to 11), bank debt has doubled and the auditor has also raised a problem about collecting debts.
Conclusion: the profit on paper is real but doesn’t reach shareholders; higher loan interest and a capital increase to cover debt are probably on the way. Off the list.
A repairer who does all their work for one big customer that doesn’t pay is busy, but borrows more every month.
This drug maker is taking 500 billion of fresh money from shareholders for a production line that is supposed to make 180 billion a year (36%).
Check: the drug pricing licence (the government sets the price), whether the last project finished on time, and the foreign currency for imported machines.
Even if profit is 30% lower, the return is about 25%; if that beats the share’s current return, it creates value. A year’s delay only makes it later.
If the partners put in 500 million and the new branch makes 180 million a year, even if it makes 126 million, it’s still a good move.
Pharma E: fresh money that builds growth
Compare two companies on transparency.
The good company: reports on time and in detail, explains any drops, announces project progress with percentages and dates, and the auditor has no important problems.
The weak company: late reports, one correction after another, the same vague text every year, and a capital increase every year for half-finished projects.
The weak company has unknown risk even at a low P/E; either don’t buy, or buy very little.
Of two car sellers, you trust the one who shows all the repair invoices, not the one who says “it’s perfect, don’t worry”.
The transparent company and the murky one
For each new report, go through these 7 steps:
1. What kind of report is it? 2. Compare it with your own earlier guess. 3. What percentage of yearly profit does it change?
4. Is it permanent or temporary? Only a permanent change changes lasting profit. 5. Update lasting profit, payback and the comparison with Akhza.
6. Is the reason you bought still there? 7. Write it in the journal before doing anything. A change under 5% usually needs no action.
Like when a new bill arrives: what bill it is, how it differs from last month, whether it’s permanent or one-off, and whether it changes the month’s budget.
7 steps for each new report
This is the same real 6-month report. Net profit grew 149%, but almost all of it came from a 41% drop in the cost of making things; sales are only 3.5% higher.
With inflation of 30 to 45%, sales actually fell.
The cost of making things may have dropped for four reasons: cheaper materials, selling a more profitable product, goods being stored, or a one-off item. The first two last; the last two don’t.
Until the reason is clear, don’t take 472 rials as lasting profit.
If a bakery had double profit for a month because it bought flour somewhere cheap, you need to ask whether the same cheap flour will be there next month.
Admin and side costs rose faster than sales.
The company paid almost no tax (an exemption). If it paid the normal 25% tax, this period’s earnings per share would be 357 rials.
Capital also grew 29%; so the real growth in earnings per share for shareholders is 94%, not 149%.
Depending on the answer to two open questions, this 6-month profit is between 128 and 472 rials. Doubling 472 for the whole year is wrong.
If your pay was high this month because tax wasn’t taken off, you can’t count the same for the whole year.
Check on Codal in this order:
The cost-of-making note (materials, wages, overhead, change in stock); this year’s monthly reports against last year’s; the tax note (type of exemption and when it ends).
Balance sheet: inventory and money owed by customers; cash from the company’s work against profit.
The capital-increase announcement (where the money came from and where it went) and the managers’ explanation in the interpretive report.
Like following up a strange bill: first the itemised bill, then previous months’ bills, then calling the office for an explanation.
